answers.question: What is the app?
answers.answer: Grocery delivery app, Kotlin on Android and Swift on iOS.

answers.question: How bad is it and where does that come from?
answers.answer: Play Store rating fell from 4.3 to 3.6 in six weeks; crash-free users on Android went from 99.4% to 97.1% (Firebase Crashlytics, reported). Most complaints mention crashes at checkout.

answers.question: What can your AI reach?
answers.answer: Crashlytics and Play Console through the browser; GitHub read and draft pull requests.

answers.question: How do releases work?
answers.answer: Staged rollout, and each release needs the mobile lead's approval.

answers.question: What counts as fixed, by when?
answers.answer: Crash-free users back above 99.3% and rating at 4.2 within two months.

research.approach: Practitioners rank crashes by the number of users affected, not event counts, then slice by app version, Android version and device to find what changed and for whom. They check the data first: stack traces must be readable (mapping files uploaded), and Crashlytics and Play's Android vitals count differently, so they pick one measure and compare like for like. Each top crash is reproduced from its stack trace before it is fixed, the fix gets a regression test, and the build ships as a staged rollout that is watched at each step against the previous version's crash rate, ANRs and new reviews. A bad rollout is halted, and because Play cannot roll back, the repair is a new build. Ratings recover with a lag, so crash-free users are the metric to steer by and the rating is read weekly.

steps.name: Pull crash, vitals, review and release data for the same period
steps.why: The drop is only readable against release dates and versions: crashes by version, vitals, reviews with their app version and the rollout history.

steps.name: Check the data can be trusted
steps.why: Unreadable stack traces, two tools that count differently, and versions without crash reporting all distort the ranking.

steps.name: Rank crashes by users affected and slice by version, OS and device
steps.why: Impact, not event count, decides the order; slicing shows which release and which users, and flags regressed issues.

steps.name: Link complaints and rating drops to crashes and versions
steps.why: Reviews that name checkout need to match a crash group and release before anyone assumes crashes cause all of the rating drop.

steps.name: Reproduce each top crash and find its cause
steps.why: The stack trace names the exception and the line; reproducing under low memory, poor network or the affected OS confirms the cause before a fix.

steps.name: Fix with a regression test, one crash group per pull request
steps.why: A failing test that reproduces the crash, then a minimal fix, keeps fixes reviewable and reversible.

steps.name: Plan the staged rollout with watch rules and a halt rule
steps.why: Small steps with hold times and a stop rule limit the damage of a bad build; Play cannot roll back, so the plan is halt and fix forward.

steps.name: Ship in stages and watch each step before increasing
steps.why: Each increase waits for crash-free users, ANRs and reviews of the new version to be no worse than the previous one.

steps.name: Read crash-free users per version, then the rating with its lag
steps.why: Crash-free users move first; ratings follow new reviews, so they are read weekly and not used to stop or accelerate a rollout.

pitfalls.text: Ranking crashes by event count, so one user in a loop outranks a crash that hits many users.
Mixing Crashlytics and Android vitals numbers: they count at different times and for different users.
Fixing from a stack trace that is not readable because mapping or symbol files were not uploaded.
Treating a halted rollout as a rollback: users who already updated stay on the bad build until a fixed release ships.
Resuming a halted rollout without a fix, or raising the percentage after one good day of thin data.
Assuming all of the rating drop is crashes and not checking the other themes in the reviews.

Every number says whether it comes from Crashlytics or Android vitals

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Record what caused the crashes and what would have caught them: release checks, a crash-free-users alert per version, mapping-file upload, staged-rollout rules. Save them with their scope and plan the next round if a target is missed.

checks.name: Each rule says whether it holds for this job, this business or the playbook
If a target was missed, the next hypotheses and the data needed are named

hypotheses.statement: A recent release introduced a crash on the checkout path: an unhandled exception such as a null value, a bad cast or state lost after rotation or process death.
hypotheses.test: Find the first-seen version of the top checkout crash groups and read the diff of that release for the changed checkout code.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The crash group first appears in the release that changed that path, with a matching stack trace.
hypotheses.refute_if: Checkout crashes existed at the same rate before the release.

hypotheses.statement: A third-party SDK or library update (payments, maps, analytics or Play Services) crashes in the checkout flow.
hypotheses.test: Compare dependency versions between releases and check whether the top frames are inside a library.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Top frames are in the library and a version changed in the release where crashes began.
hypotheses.refute_if: Top frames are in app code and dependencies did not change.

hypotheses.statement: The crashes are concentrated on particular Android versions or devices, for example a new OS release or low-memory phones.
hypotheses.test: Slice each top crash group by Android version, device model and memory-related exceptions.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A small set of OS versions or devices holds most of the affected users.
hypotheses.refute_if: Crashes are spread evenly across OS versions and devices.

hypotheses.statement: Checkout crashes come from unhandled network errors or a server response the app cannot parse, which a backend change could also cause.
hypotheses.test: Read the exception types, check custom keys and logs for request failures, and compare the crash timing with backend releases.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Exceptions are network or parsing errors and line up with poor-connection users or a backend change.
hypotheses.refute_if: Exceptions are local null, cast or lifecycle errors.

hypotheses.statement: A minification or obfuscation change in a recent release removed code that the app loads at runtime.
hypotheses.test: Look for class-not-found or reflection exceptions that begin in one release, and compare the build settings between releases.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Such exceptions begin in a release that changed build or keep rules.

hypotheses.statement: Part of the drop is a measurement effect: a version without crash reporting, a change in collection, or ANRs and crashes counted together.
hypotheses.test: Check SDK coverage by version and compare Crashlytics with Android vitals for the same versions.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Coverage or definitions changed in the period when the figure fell.
hypotheses.refute_if: Both tools show the same fall on the same versions.

hypotheses.statement: Not all of the rating drop is from crashes: other themes in the reviews (delivery, pricing, bugs outside checkout) also pull it down.
hypotheses.test: Classify the last 90 days of reviews by theme and version and compare the star distribution before and after the drop.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A large share of low-star reviews do not mention crashes.
hypotheses.refute_if: Nearly all low-star reviews name crashes or checkout failures.

measurement.window: Crash-free users per version after each rollout step and for at least two weeks after the last fix reaches 100%; the rating weekly for the rest of the two months.
measurement.min_volume: Enough users on the new version for a stable crash-free figure at each step; below that, report INCONCLUSIVE and hold the step.
measurement.stop_rule: Halt the rollout if the new version's crash-free users, ANR rate or new reviews are worse than the previous version's at a step, and fix forward in a new build; the mobile lead decides whether to resume.
